A0232.title: Robot Safety Stop E-stop & Functional-Safety Design
keywords: robot safety stop E-stop & functional-safety design
A0232.definition: Hardware-level emergency-stop loops, safety controllers, collaborative-robot force and speed limits, and ISO 10218/ISO/TS 15066 compliant functional-safety design to ensure robots can stop quickly and limit physical harm under anomalies.
A0232.description:
Robot safety stop E-stop & functional-safety design builds hardware-to-architecture defense-in-depth against robot physical-harm and functional-safety failure. First, hardware-level emergency-stop loops are independent of the software control link; pressing cuts motor power and software faults cannot bypass them. Second, safety controllers use redundant architectures and self-diagnostics to execute safety-interlock monitoring (light curtains, safety mats, safety doors). Third, collaborative-robot force and speed limits comply with ISO/TS 15066 human-robot collaboration pressure thresholds, proactively decelerating before collision. Fourth, functional-safety design follows ISO 10218 (industrial-robot safety), ISO 13482 (personal-care robot safety), with risk assessment and safety-level (PLd/SIL2) design.

This measure is the core physical-safety defense after incidents like Knightscope K5 collisions and the Volkswagen Baunatal fatality; it works with A0147 (industrial protocol hardening) and A0014 (tamper-proofing).
A0232.limitation: Hardware e-stop cannot handle already-applied mechanical inertia; high-speed motion still has braking distance; functional-safety certification is costly and long, hard for SMBs; soft e-stop can be bypassed by software faults, requiring hardware e-stop as backstop; force and speed limits reduce task efficiency, requiring fine tuning in collaboration scenarios.
